label: Affine and Riemannian Connections
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 48 through 59 and introduces the connection, the device that lets us differentiate one vector field along another on a manifold. We motivate why naive coordinate differentiation fails and preview the unique Levi-Civita connection that closes the chapter.

label: Why Differentiation Needs a Connection
notes: On a surface the ordinary derivative of a tangent field leaves the tangent plane, so it is not intrinsic. A connection supplies the missing rule that projects the change back into the tangent space, making directional differentiation a well defined manifold operation.

label: Definition of an Affine Connection
notes: An affine connection assigns to each pair of fields a new field, linear over functions in the first slot and a derivation obeying the Leibniz rule in the second. These three axioms are exactly what is needed for a coordinate-free notion of directional derivative.

label: Christoffel Symbols in Coordinates
notes: In a chart the connection is encoded by the Christoffel symbols, the components of the covariant derivative of one basis field along another. Everything about the connection in that chart is recovered from these functions, which need not be tensor components.

label: Covariant Derivative Along a Curve
notes: Restricting a field to a curve, the connection induces a derivative of that field with respect to the curve parameter. Its coordinate expression couples the ordinary derivative of the components with the Christoffel symbols evaluated along the velocity.

label: Parallel Transport
notes: A field is parallel along a curve when its covariant derivative vanishes identically. This linear differential equation has a unique solution for each initial vector, defining parallel transport, the connection-dependent way to carry tangent vectors between points along a path.

label: Compatibility with the Metric
notes: A connection is compatible with the Riemannian metric when parallel transport preserves inner products, equivalently when the metric is covariantly constant. This makes lengths and angles invariant under transport and ties the connection to the geometry of the manifold.

label: Symmetry and Torsion
notes: A connection is symmetric, or torsion-free, when the covariant derivative is symmetric in its two arguments up to the Lie bracket. In coordinates this says the lower Christoffel indices are symmetric, ruling out any antisymmetric twisting term.

label: Fundamental Theorem
notes: Levi-Civita's theorem states that on any Riemannian manifold there is exactly one connection that is both symmetric and compatible with the metric. Existence and uniqueness together single out the Riemannian connection as the canonical derivative of the geometry.

label: The Koszul Formula
notes: The Koszul formula expresses the metric inner product of the covariant derivative purely in terms of the metric, bracket derivatives, and Lie brackets of the three fields. Because the right side is fixed, the connection it defines is forced to be unique.

label: Christoffel Symbols from the Metric
notes: Specializing Koszul to a coordinate basis yields the classical formula giving the Christoffel symbols as combinations of first derivatives of the metric components. This is the working recipe by which the Levi-Civita connection is computed in practice.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We assembled the connection from axioms, read it through Christoffel symbols, transported vectors with it, and imposed compatibility and symmetry to obtain the unique Levi-Civita connection. Geodesics and curvature in later chapters are built directly on this machinery.
